Blackboard bold, off the blackboard

The doubled stroke started as a workaround. A lecturer at a blackboard could not produce the bold of printed type, so the stem got drawn twice, and the convention stuck well enough that Unicode encoded it at U+1D538. Seven of the letters were already there: ℂ ℍ ℕ ℙ ℚ ℝ and ℤ, the number sets themselves, live in Letterlike Symbols and get reused. Digits exist too, at U+1D7D8, which is more than most alphabets here can claim.

For a note about the reals or the integers in a chat window with no formula support, this is the shortest path from thought to message. Outside maths it reads as a hollow outline face and works for a short heading. The seven borrowed letters can look a shade heavier or narrower than their neighbours, and outline forms thin out badly at small sizes, so a whole paragraph of it is hard work.

Where Double-Struck text works, and where it does not

WorksWorks in most bios, posts, display names and chat — X, Instagram, TikTok, Discord, Reddit. Watch outRefused by real-name fields (Facebook, LinkedIn's name field) and unsearchable: these are separate characters from ordinary letters, so nobody will find you by typing your name.

Double-Struck questions

Why is it called blackboard bold?

Printed maths books set the number sets in bold. Chalk cannot do bold, so lecturers copying those symbols onto a board doubled one stroke of each letter instead, and students copied the doubling back into their notes. The look outlived the problem, and Unicode eventually gave it its own characters.

Which letters come from a different block, and does it matter?

C, H, N, P, Q, R and Z were encoded earlier in Letterlike Symbols, so the run at U+1D538 skips them. It matters only visually: a font may draw those seven with a slightly different weight or width than the rest. In maths they are the letters you want most, and they are the best supported.

Can I use this for maths in a chat with no LaTeX?

For naming the sets, yes, and it beats writing R with a bar in front. It stops there. The shape is baked into each character rather than applied by a font, so you get letters and nothing else: no exponents, no fractions, no proper subscripts, and screen readers will make a mess of the line.
